threads.malleability: Malleability & equivocation — two valid versions of one thing
threads.state-transition: The state-transition function, from δ to the EVM

nodes.label: P2P gossip network
nodes.blurb: Peers flood transactions and blocks to each other with only best-effort delivery. No central server; anyone may join.

nodes.label: Hash function
nodes.blurb: A one-way, collision-resistant map from any input to a fixed-size digest whose bits look random (avalanche). SHA-256 in Bitcoin, Keccak-256 in Ethereum.

nodes.label: Digital signature
nodes.blurb: Sign(sk, m) → σ; Verify(pk, m, σ). Unforgeable without sk. Authorises every transaction and every validator vote.

nodes.label: State-transition function δ
nodes.blurb: δ(state, tx) → state'. Deterministic, so every honest node computes the same next state. Instantiated as UTXO consumption, then as the EVM.

nodes.label: Commitment
nodes.blurb: Publish H(m) now, reveal m later. Binding (can't change m) from collision resistance; hiding needs a random nonce. Used in P2PKH and P2SH.

nodes.label: Merkle tree
nodes.blurb: Hash a list in pairs up to one 32-byte root. Changing any element changes the root. The odd-row duplicate rule caused CVE-2012-2459.

nodes.label: Merkle proof / SPV
nodes.blurb: ≈ log₂n sibling hashes prove a transaction is under a given root, so a light client needs only block headers.

nodes.label: Proof of work
nodes.blurb: Find a nonce with SHA-256d(header) ≤ target. Expected work 2²⁵⁶/target. Makes block proposal costly and picks the proposer in proportion to hash power.

nodes.label: ECDSA malleability
nodes.blurb: Given (r, s), the pair (r, n−s) is also a valid signature. It never lets you steal, but it changes the legacy txid.

nodes.label: Equivocation
nodes.blurb: Showing two conflicting valid messages to different peers — the characteristic Byzantine move, and the thing consensus must survive.

nodes.label: HD wallet (BIP32/39)
nodes.blurb: One random seed (12–24 words) deterministically derives a whole tree of keys, so a single phrase backs up every address.

nodes.label: UTXO model
nodes.blurb: No accounts or balances: value lives in unspent outputs, each locked by a script. A transaction destroys some and creates others.

nodes.label: Outpoint
nodes.blurb: (txid, index) — names exactly which output is being spent. Spending it once makes a replay impossible; the account model needs an explicit nonce for this.

nodes.label: Transaction structure
nodes.blurb: Inputs (each an outpoint + unlocking script) and outputs (value + locking script), plus version and locktime.

nodes.label: Coinbase & halving
nodes.blurb: The one transaction with no real input. Pays the block reward (halving every 210 000 blocks) plus all fees; the only source of new bitcoin.

nodes.label: The three checks
nodes.blurb: Existence (input is an unspent UTXO), conservation (Σin ≥ Σout), authorisation (unlocking script runs true).

nodes.label: Transaction fees
nodes.blurb: Implicit: Σinputs − Σoutputs. A per-byte auction for scarce block space.

nodes.label: Bitcoin Script
nodes.blurb: A stack machine with no loops, so a validator can bound its cost from the script length alone. Contrast: the EVM has loops and needs gas.

nodes.label: P2PKH
nodes.blurb: OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <pkh> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG. The public key stays hidden until the first spend.

nodes.label: Multisig / escrow
nodes.blurb: t-of-n signatures. A 2-of-3 with a neutral third key is escrow where the judge never holds the money.

nodes.label: Hash-lock / atomic swap
nodes.blurb: Spend requires revealing x with SHA256(x) = h. Two of these with the same h on two chains make a trustless swap.

nodes.label: Time-locks (CLTV)
nodes.blurb: An output that can't be spent until a given block height or time — e.g. an inheritance vault.

nodes.label: Mempool
nodes.blurb: Each node's pool of valid, unconfirmed transactions. A transaction here is public but not yet settled.

nodes.label: 80-byte block header
nodes.blurb: version, prev-hash, Merkle root, time, bits (target), nonce. The chain is really the chain of these headers.

nodes.label: Prev-hash link
nodes.blurb: Each header commits to the hash of the one before it, so editing an old block breaks every block after it.

nodes.label: Difficulty & retargeting
nodes.blurb: The target is rescaled every 2016 blocks so blocks arrive about every 10 minutes as total hash power changes.

nodes.label: SegWit
nodes.blurb: Moves signatures into a separate witness not covered by the txid — fixing malleability — and adds weight units.

nodes.label: Byzantine Generals
nodes.blurb: n parties, some traitors, must agree on one value over unreliable messengers. Needs Agreement, Validity, Termination.

nodes.label: Byzantine Broadcast
nodes.blurb: One sender, everyone agrees on its value even if the sender is malicious and equivocates. Dolev–Strong solves it in f+1 rounds.

nodes.label: State machine replication
nodes.blurb: Run agreement block after block to build one common, ordered log. Replicas run the protocol; clients read the log.

nodes.label: Safety & liveness
nodes.blurb: Safety: no two honest nodes' logs ever conflict. Liveness: an honestly-received transaction eventually appears in every log.

nodes.label: Double-spend
nodes.blurb: One coin, two conflicting recipients. A safety failure — the concrete harm consensus exists to prevent.

nodes.label: Sybil resistance
nodes.blurb: Stop one attacker minting many identities to outvote everyone. Tie voting power to a scarce resource: work, or stake.

nodes.label: Nakamoto consensus
nodes.blurb: Three rules: PoW leader election, build on the heaviest chain, treat k-deep as settled.

nodes.label: Heaviest-chain rule
nodes.blurb: When there are competing branches, extend the one with the most cumulative work.

nodes.label: Confirmation depth k
nodes.blurb: How many blocks must sit on top before a transaction is treated as final. k ≈ 6 in practice.

nodes.label: 51% / private attack
nodes.blurb: Mine a hidden chain and release it once it's longer, reversing a confirmed transaction. Succeeds for sure only with ≥ 50% hash power.

nodes.label: Security theorem
nodes.blurb: If the adversary has < 50% and blocks are slow enough, reversal probability falls like e^(−Ω(k)).

nodes.label: Block reward + fees
nodes.blurb: What pays miners — but only for blocks on the heaviest chain, which is what makes honest mining an equilibrium.

nodes.label: Selfish mining
nodes.blurb: Withhold found blocks to waste others' work. Profitable above roughly 25–33% share (0% if perfectly connected) — honest mining being most profitable is an assumption, not a theorem.

nodes.label: Proof of stake / slashing
nodes.blurb: Lock coins to vote; misbehaviour burns the stake. Validators are accountable because the stake is on-chain and forfeitable.

nodes.label: Finality
nodes.blurb: A finalised block cannot be reverted without a provable, slashable fault by ≥ 1/3 of stake. Bitcoin has no finality, only depth.

nodes.label: Blockchain CAP theorem
nodes.blurb: No protocol is both dynamically available and final under a network partition. Ethereum nests a finalised chain inside an available one.

nodes.label: Account model
nodes.blurb: State is a map from address to { balance, nonce, code, storage }. Payments edit balances in place.

nodes.label: Account nonce
nodes.blurb: A per-account counter that must increase by one each transaction — the anti-replay role Bitcoin's outpoint plays.

nodes.label: EOA vs contract
nodes.blurb: An EOA is controlled by a key and starts every transaction; a contract account is controlled by fixed code and only runs when called.

nodes.label: EVM
nodes.blurb: A stack machine like Script but with jumps (loops) and persistent storage. Because it can loop, its cost must be metered.

nodes.label: Gas
nodes.blurb: Every instruction has a fixed gas price. Run out and the transaction reverts — but the gas is still charged.

nodes.label: EIP-1559 base fee
nodes.blurb: A per-block base fee that adjusts with demand and is burned; a tip goes to the proposer. Burning removes the off-chain rebate lever.

nodes.label: Solidity contracts
nodes.blurb: Statically-typed language compiled to EVM bytecode: state variables, functions, modifiers, events, inheritance.

nodes.label: Reentrancy
nodes.blurb: An external call lets the callee re-enter before the caller updates the state meant to stop reuse. Drained the DAO in 2016.

nodes.label: Checks-effects-interactions
nodes.blurb: Do all checks, then all state updates, then any external call. The standard fix for reentrancy.

nodes.label: The DAO → Ethereum Classic
nodes.blurb: The 2016 hack that drained ~3.6M ETH via reentrancy, and the contentious hard fork that split the chain.
